paragraphs: People perceive movement over both short and long distances in complex scenes. Earlier explanations assumed that these forms of motion perception required separate mechanisms. This paper proposes a hierarchical model that handles both within one framework, asking whether a shared set of computational principles can account for the observed human responses.

The model combines two sources of information. A data likelihood uses nonlinear matching to propose several possible interpretations of motion. A hierarchical prior then constrains those interpretations through preferences for slowness and spatial smoothness at multiple scales. This lets the model consider ambiguous movement evidence while favoring motion fields that satisfy these organizing constraints.

The authors test the framework using random dot kinematograms and multiple-aperture stimuli, two stimulus types used in human vision research. They report that the model adequately accounts for human performance in the psychophysical experiments. These findings support the proposed framework as a unified explanation of the tested behaviors, without establishing that it is the actual mechanism implemented by human vision.
neurips-2010-a-unified-model-of-short-ra.tldr: A hierarchical motion model accounts for tested human responses to both short-range and long-range movement.

paragraphs: Neural-network learning can spend a long time on a plateau where the objective barely changes. This paper studies plateaus associated with singularities in the parameter space. Such regions can attract first-order gradient learning and look like local minima, even though their geometry may offer directions that allow further descent.

The analysis examines the Hessian, which describes curvature of the objective with respect to the parameters. Near perturbed singular points, this matrix tends to have both positive and negative curvature directions. That finding suggests using negative curvature to escape plateaus: the surrounding objective can contain a descending direction that ordinary gradient updates do not exploit effectively.

The numerical evidence is explicitly restricted to small examples where the authors can verify the singularities and Hessian eigenvalues. In those examples, descent using a negative-curvature direction encounters no plateau. The results support a promising optimization strategy and explain why an apparently flat region can be misleading, while the stated demonstrations remain limited to these inspectable small problems.
neurips-2010-an-analysis-on-negative-cur.tldr: Negative curvature near neural-network singularities suggests a way to escape training plateaus, supported by small numerical examples.

paragraphs: Arithmetic circuits can make exact probabilistic inference manageable by exploiting determinism and independence that holds in particular contexts. These properties can help even when a network has high treewidth. This paper extends the circuit approach to approximate inference for domains where exact inference remains computationally impractical.

The authors investigate several routes to constructing and using these approximations. Their techniques draw on exact compilation, forward sampling, circuit structure learning, Markov network parameter learning, variational inference, and Gibbs sampling. The central question is which combinations make arithmetic circuits useful when their usual exact-inference role is insufficient.

Experiments across eight challenging real-world domains favor methods that combine sampling and learning. AC2-F is faster and usually more accurate than loopy belief propagation, mean field, and Gibbs sampling in those experiments. AC2-G takes a similar amount of time to Gibbs sampling but is consistently more accurate than all evaluated baselines. These findings identify two empirically effective circuit-based options with different reported runtime and accuracy profiles.
neurips-2010-approximate-inference-by-co.tldr: Sampling and learning make arithmetic circuits effective approximate-inference tools in eight tested real-world domains.

paragraphs: An evolving mixture model needs to represent groups whose composition and locations can change over time. This paper constructs a sequence of dependent Dirichlet processes to serve as a prior for such models. The aim is to connect successive distributions while retaining the Dirichlet-process form at each individual time.

The construction uses a relationship between Dirichlet processes and Poisson processes to build a Markov chain of random measures. Within that chain, mixture components can appear, disappear, or change location. Despite these changes and the dependence between successive measures, each measure remains marginally distributed as a Dirichlet process. The construction therefore combines temporal evolution with a preserved distributional property.

The authors also derive a Gibbs sampling algorithm for inference, providing a way to fit the evolving model to observations. They evaluate it on synthetic and real data and report effective estimation of dynamically changing mixtures. The contribution connects a probabilistic construction with an inference procedure and empirical evidence that the resulting model can track mixture evolution.
neurips-2010-construction-of-dependent-d.tldr: A Poisson-process construction lets Dirichlet-process mixtures evolve while preserving their marginal distributional form.

paragraphs: CUR approximates a matrix using a representation that lies in the span of a small selection of its columns. This gives it a form of sparsity alongside low reconstruction error. The resemblance to sparse principal component analysis raises a natural question: are these methods solving essentially the same kind of optimization problem?

The paper investigates CUR through sparse optimization rather than only through its randomized algorithm. The authors show that CUR implicitly optimizes a sparse regression objective. They also show that it cannot be directly reformulated as a sparse PCA method. The distinction matters because similar-looking sparse representations do not by themselves imply equivalent underlying objectives.

The analysis then becomes a source of a new method. The authors identify a particular structure in the sparsity produced by CUR and formulate a sparse PCA approach that achieves a similar structure. Thus, the paper both clarifies the relationship between two matrix approximation approaches and transfers a useful representational property from CUR into a sparse PCA formulation.
neurips-2010-cur-from-a-sparse-optimizat.tldr: CUR implicitly solves a sparse regression problem, and its sparsity structure inspires a new sparse PCA formulation.

paragraphs: This paper asks how useful representations can be learned when only subsampled measurements of a signal are available. The proposed algorithm learns sparse representations without supervision and estimates the parameters needed to reconstruct signals linearly from those representations. Learning the code and learning how to decode it are therefore both parts of the approach.

The authors report compression efficiency comparable to compressive sampling. They also demonstrate robust performance when several stages are stacked together and in both undercomplete and overcomplete settings. These evaluations address whether the method remains useful across different representation sizes and when processing is repeated through multiple stages.

The paper connects this computational result to communication between neural populations. Fiber bottlenecks mean that a population may receive subsampled input, yet still develop coherent response properties. The algorithm offers a possible explanation for how that can happen: sparse representations and reconstruction parameters can be learned from restricted measurements. This is presented as an explanatory possibility, rather than proof that the brain uses the proposed algorithm.
neurips-2010-deciphering-subsampled-data.tldr: An unsupervised algorithm learns sparse codes from subsampled inputs and offers a possible account of communication through neural bottlenecks.

paragraphs: Multi-view learning combines different input modalities that can contain both common and modality-specific information. Factorized latent representations separate those contributions, helping describe which aspects of the inputs depend on one another. This paper develops a sparse-coding-inspired approach to learning that separation.

The method uses structured sparsity and alternates between two convex optimization problems. This gives the learning procedure convex subproblems; it does not amount to a claim that the complete joint optimization is convex. The representation also expands the available sharing patterns: a latent dimension can belong to any subset of views, instead of being restricted to either one view or every view.

That flexibility matters when different groups of modalities share different information. It provides a richer way to express dependencies and independencies within the same latent space. On human pose estimation, the authors report performance exceeding the state-of-the-art methods they compare against. The stated result supplies empirical support for the approach in that task, alongside its more general representational contribution.
neurips-2010-factorized-latent-spaces-wi.tldr: Structured sparsity learns latent features shared by arbitrary subsets of views and improves the reported human pose estimation results.

paragraphs: Inverse reinforcement learning seeks a reward function from examples of an optimal policy in a Markov decision process. Existing techniques generally depend on a concise set of reward features supplied by a user. This paper addresses the feature-design step by constructing relevant reward features from a larger collection of components.

The algorithm builds logical conjunctions of component features, combining conditions into features that matter to the example policy. Given demonstration traces, it returns both the constructed features and a reward function. This makes the representation of the reward an explicit output of learning, rather than requiring that representation to be fully specified beforehand.

The resulting reward can be used to recover a complete policy that is deterministic and stationary. The constructed features also support moving the reward to another environment, provided the component features are well defined there. That qualification is central to the transfer claim: the method supplies a reusable feature-based description of the reward, with transfer tied to the availability of those components in the new setting.
neurips-2010-feature-construction-for-in.tldr: The method constructs reward features from demonstrations and supports reward transfer where the underlying component features remain defined.

paragraphs: An object-detection cascade saves computation by rejecting easy negative image regions early. Only regions that survive the initial classifiers receive further evaluation. This paper develops a way to train the classifiers jointly, so that learning directly addresses the combined response of the cascade.

Each classifier's output is interpreted as a probability of a positive prediction. The cascade output represents the probability that every classifier predicts positively, giving a probabilistic AND model. From this model, the authors derive a consistent loss and a boosting procedure that optimizes the overall probability on the training data.

Joint optimization lets individual predictors concentrate on more restricted modeling problems while contributing to the cascade's collective decision. The authors report improved performance relative to a standard cascade and demonstrate efficiency on face and pedestrian detection using standard datasets and reference baselines. The contribution therefore links the computational advantage of early rejection with an objective that coordinates the classifiers during training, with empirical support in the two stated detection applications.
neurips-2010-joint-cascade-optimization-.tldr: A probabilistic AND objective trains boosted cascade classifiers jointly and improves reported face and pedestrian detection performance.

paragraphs: Sparse visual features are often learned from separate image patches and then applied across an image. The paper identifies a source of redundancy in this workflow: overlapping patches are encoded independently during training. Its unsupervised method instead trains convolutionally over larger image windows, reducing redundancy between neighboring feature vectors.

The system learns both a linear decoder, which reconstructs images from sparse features, and a feed-forward encoder, which efficiently predicts approximately sparse features from an input. This pairs a reconstruction-based representation with a direct way to compute features. The approach also supports learning multiple stages of a feature hierarchy.

The authors report a more diverse collection of learned filters than the predominantly oriented edge detectors associated with patch-based training. Their filters include center-surround patterns, corners, crosses, and oriented gratings. Using these filters in multi-stage convolutional networks improves performance on several visual recognition and detection tasks. The findings connect a change in the spatial scope of training to less redundant representations, greater filter diversity, and better evaluated task performance.
neurips-2010-learning-convolutional-feat.tldr: Training sparse features convolutionally over larger image windows reduces redundancy and improves evaluated visual recognition and detection.

paragraphs: The paper studies reinforcement learning when the feature representation has more dimensions than there are samples. It focuses on least-squares temporal difference learning, or LSTD, after a random projection maps the original features into a lower-dimensional space. The question is how this reduction affects the resulting learning procedure.

The authors provide a theoretical analysis and derive performance bounds for LSTD with random projections. These bounds give a formal way to assess the quality of the projected method. The contribution is therefore more than introducing a smaller representation: it analyzes the consequences of using that representation within temporal difference learning.

The analysis then follows the error through repeated policy-iteration steps and provides a performance bound for the resulting least-squares policy iteration algorithm. This extension matters because error in one learning step can influence later steps that build on its output. By treating both the projected LSTD procedure and its role inside policy iteration, the paper connects dimensionality reduction to the performance of the broader reinforcement-learning process.
neurips-2010-lstd-with-random-projection.tldr: The paper bounds the performance of randomly projected LSTD and analyzes how its error propagates through policy iteration.

paragraphs: This paper addresses finding a most probable assignment in a binary Markov random field with pairwise potentials. It proposes a new linear programming relaxation, obtained by translating the assignment problem into a bipartite multi-cut problem. The relaxation supplies an optimization route to the original discrete inference task.

The stated approximation guarantee is O(log k), where k counts vertices adjacent to non-submodular edges in the original model. Thus, the guarantee depends on a specific structural quantity. The authors also introduce a combinatorial algorithm to solve the linear program efficiently while approximately solving its dual, which provides a lower bound alongside the optimization result.

In the reported comparison, the algorithm is up to an order of magnitude faster and gives better MAP scores and bounds than a state-of-the-art message-passing method that uses third-order marginal constraints. These results combine two benefits: improved candidate assignments and improved bounds for assessing them. The runtime claim describes the observed comparison, while the approximation guarantee is expressed through the stated parameter k.
neurips-2010-map-estimation-in-binary-mr.tldr: A bipartite multi-cut relaxation provides approximation guarantees and improves reported speed, MAP scores, and bounds for binary MRF inference.

paragraphs: Sequential Minimal Optimization, or SMO, is an established way to train support vector machines because it is simple and scales efficiently. Applying the same strategy to multiple kernel learning has been difficult: the standard dual objective is not differentiable, preventing the usual SMO-style coordinate-ascent approach.

The paper shows that linear multiple kernel learning can use SMO when regularized by the squared p-norm or by certain Bregman divergences. This is a qualified result about particular regularizers, rather than all possible multiple-kernel objectives. It gives those formulations access to a training procedure valued for its implementation simplicity and efficiency.

The resulting algorithm is reported to be significantly faster than specialized state-of-the-art p-norm multiple-kernel solvers. The authors demonstrate training with one hundred thousand kernels in about seven minutes and with fifty thousand points in under half an hour, using a single core. These examples establish the reported scale of the method and show why resolving the optimization obstacle matters in practice.
neurips-2010-multiple-kernel-learning-an.tldr: Squared p-norm and certain Bregman regularizers make linear multiple kernel learning compatible with efficient SMO training.

paragraphs: Multitask learning often assumes that tasks use the same labels or that someone can supply a mapping between their label sets. This paper tackles the setting where label sets may differ and their correspondences are not readily available. The goal is to learn across tasks without requiring either of those starting conditions.

The method directly maximizes mutual information among the labels. This provides a way to express relationships between label spaces without first requiring identical label names or an externally supplied correspondence. The authors show that existing algorithms can efficiently optimize the resulting objective, connecting the proposed formulation to available optimization machinery.

A stated application is integrating classification data from differently organized web directories, such as Yahoo! and DMOZ. Their distinct label spaces illustrate why a shared-label assumption can obstruct data integration. The contribution is an algorithmic formulation for this mismatch: it makes dependence among labels the quantity to optimize, allowing the learning problem to be posed even when a label mapping is unavailable.
neurips-2010-multitask-learning-without-.tldr: Mutual-information optimization enables multitask learning with potentially different label sets and no supplied label correspondence.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes statistical convergence for kernel least-squares regression solved with conjugate gradients. The method controls overfitting by stopping the iterative algorithm early. It is directly related to Kernel Partial Least Squares, connecting supervised dimensionality reduction with least-squares projection.

The learning rates depend on the regularity of the target function and the effective dimensionality of the data in kernel space. When the true regression function belongs to the reproducing kernel Hilbert space, the authors obtain upper bounds matching previously established lower bounds up to a logarithmic factor. This makes the optimality claim conditional on that function-space assumption and qualified by the logarithmic difference.

When the target does not belong to that space, the paper obtains similar rates provided additional unlabeled data are available. In both settings, the orders of the rates match contemporary results for least-squares support vector machines and linear regularization operators. The findings give early stopping in conjugate-gradient regression a statistical justification, showing how its accuracy guarantees relate to properties of the target and the data.
neurips-2010-optimal-learning-rates-for-.tldr: Early-stopped kernel conjugate-gradient regression achieves near-optimal statistical rates under the stated function-space or unlabeled-data conditions.

paragraphs: As datasets grow, distributing learning across parallel computation becomes increasingly important. This paper presents a parallel stochastic gradient descent algorithm supported by both a detailed analysis and experiments. Its contribution includes guarantees of parallel acceleration, making the speed benefit part of the theoretical treatment rather than solely an experimental observation.

The proposed variant avoids overly tight latency requirements of the kind that might be practical only in a multicore setting. This addresses a constraint on where parallel optimization can be useful. The abstract does not make the stronger claim that communication timing is irrelevant; it states that the required latency conditions are not excessively restrictive.

The analysis uses contractive mappings to measure how quickly distributions of the algorithm's parameters approach their asymptotic limits. This distributional perspective also answers how quickly stochastic gradient descent reaches its asymptotically normal regime. The paper therefore contributes both a parallel learning method with acceleration guarantees and a proof technique that yields insight into the statistical behavior of stochastic gradient descent.
neurips-2010-parallelized-stochastic-gra.tldr: A parallel SGD algorithm comes with acceleration guarantees and an analysis of how quickly parameter distributions approach their asymptotic behavior.

paragraphs: The max-norm is a convex matrix regularizer with earlier empirical evidence of advantages over the trace-norm in collaborative filtering. Its practical use faced an optimization barrier: polynomial-time computability did not provide an effective method for large problems involving the regularizer. This paper addresses that gap between theoretical tractability and usable computation.

The authors apply a matrix factorization technique to develop scalable first-order algorithms for convex programs involving the max-norm. The factorization is the means of making these optimization problems manageable at larger scales. The work therefore focuses on how to compute with an existing regularizer, rather than proposing the max-norm itself.

The algorithms are applied to very large collaborative filtering, graph cut, and clustering problems. Across all three areas, the authors report better empirical performance than mature techniques. Those results support the practical value of the optimization approach in several distinct applications. They also show how improving the solver can broaden access to a regularizer whose computational formulation had previously limited large-scale use.
neurips-2010-practical-large-scale-optim.tldr: Factorization-based first-order algorithms make max-norm optimization practical at large scales and outperform evaluated methods in three application areas.

paragraphs: The paper develops a random-walk method for online convex optimization and repeated games. In these settings, decisions are made over time, and low regret is a way to assess their cumulative quality. The proposed algorithm connects that sequential decision problem to efficient sampling within a convex body.

Its central property is rapid mixing toward a Gibbs distribution that changes over time. Mixing describes how the random walk approaches the target distribution. The moving target is important here: the method is designed to follow an evolving distribution, rather than only approximate a single fixed one. The abstract states that this process is computationally efficient.

Applied to online optimization and repeated games, the algorithm yields low regret and provides an efficient implementation of mixture forecasting strategies. The contribution brings together the quality of sequential decisions and the computation needed to produce them. A rapidly mixing walk supplies the computational mechanism, while the low-regret result connects that mechanism to the forecasting and game-playing settings identified in the paper.
neurips-2010-random-walk-approach-to-reg.tldr: An efficient random walk tracks changing Gibbs distributions to implement mixture forecasting with low regret.

paragraphs: This paper defines clusters through affinity relations involving groups of objects. A cluster is a subset with high average affinity, and the formulation accommodates relations among two or more objects. It therefore covers both graph-based clustering with pairwise relations and hypergraph-based clustering with relations involving larger groups.

The authors relax the average-affinity objective and approximate it with a constrained homogeneous function, then provide an efficient optimization procedure. They also use priors systematically constructed from the data to reveal the underlying clusters. These components turn the affinity-based definition into a procedure for selecting groups of objects.

A key property is that the method can leave some points ungrouped rather than assigning every point to a cluster. This provides its stated resistance to large numbers of outliers, which need not be absorbed into the selected groups. The paper reports theoretical and experimental advantages over classical clustering solutions, especially in outlier-heavy settings. The contribution combines this selective grouping behavior with a common formulation for pairwise and higher-order affinities.
neurips-2010-robust-clustering-as-ensemb.tldr: Affinity-based clustering can leave points ungrouped, supporting robustness to many outliers across graph and hypergraph settings.

paragraphs: Different low-level segmentations of one image provide competing candidate regions. This paper selects visually meaningful regions from that ensemble without knowing which specific objects or surfaces are present. It constructs a graph from the candidate segments and poses selection as a maximum-weight independent set problem.

The selected set contains mutually non-adjacent graph nodes with high combined weight. In the paper's construction, this identifies distinctive segments that together partition the image. The proposed solver works directly with discrete solutions, repeatedly using a Taylor expansion of the objective around the preceding solution. The authors show convergence to a maximum, without stating that this is necessarily the global maximum.

On the Berkeley segmentation benchmark, the method removes the need to hand-pick optimal input parameters for the evaluated state-of-the-art segmenters and exceeds their best manually optimized results. This demonstrates the value of selecting regions across an ensemble rather than relying on one parameter choice. The graph formulation links that selection task to a discrete optimization method with a stated convergence result.
neurips-2010-segmentation-as-maximum-wei.tldr: Discrete graph optimization selects image regions from multiple segmentations and beats the reported manually tuned results on the Berkeley benchmark.

paragraphs: A distribution over probability mass functions must describe which probability vectors are plausible. The paper argues that the Dirichlet distribution's component dependence structure limits its accuracy for some problems. It introduces the shadow Dirichlet family to represent probability mass functions with additional dependencies or restrictions.

The approach changes the support: the set of probability vectors that the distribution can assign mass to. This provides a way to model requirements such as monotonicity, regularization, or bounded variation. The central idea is to incorporate restrictions into the distribution's allowed configurations, making the model reflect structure among the probabilities themselves.

The authors describe properties of the new family and provide maximum-entropy constructions. They also develop an expectation-maximization procedure for estimating its mean parameter and illustrate the approach with real data. These contributions cover both defining the restricted probability model and estimating a key parameter from observations. Together, they offer modeling and inference tools for settings where the stated dependencies or constraints are important features of a probability mass function.
neurips-2010-shadow-dirichlet-for-restri.tldr: Shadow Dirichlet distributions modify support to model constrained probability vectors, with maximum-entropy constructions and an EM estimation method.

paragraphs: The paper treats identifying basic code blocks in an executable as a sequence-segmentation problem. The input is a sequence of bytes, and the learned output divides that sequence into segments. This turns a binary-analysis task into a structured prediction problem whose output must describe an entire sequence.

General segmentation models can require inference time that grows cubically with sequence length. That is a serious obstacle when even small executables contain tens or hundreds of thousands of bytes. By exploiting the structure of this particular problem, the authors derive an inference algorithm whose time grows linearly with sequence length, making the approach practical for these long inputs.

The authors also introduce two loss functions tailored to the task and show how structural support vector machines can optimize the learned mapping for them. Experiments demonstrate advantages over a strong baseline. The work combines task-specific prediction criteria with efficient inference, addressing both what kinds of segmentation errors training should penalize and how to compute predictions at the required scale.
neurips-2010-static-analysis-of-binary-e.tldr: Structural SVMs learn executable-byte segmentations using task-specific losses and a practical linear-time inference algorithm.

paragraphs: A subject wore a camera for two weeks, producing an image roughly every twenty seconds. The paper seeks an unsupervised summary of this visual record, with the goal of discovering recurring scenes, familiar faces, or common actions. Dataset size and substantial lighting variation make direct use of existing stitching and appearance-clustering approaches impractical.

The proposed representation, called a stel epitome, maps images or patches into a shared epitome matrix. Its limited space forces mappings from different images to overlap, with overlap expressing similarity. The crucial change is how similarity is represented: it depends on the spatial arrangement of scene or object parts rather than direct comparisons of pixel intensities, colors, or features.

The model is based on palette-invariant representations and comes with an efficient learning algorithm. It captures structure despite non-structural changes, such as illumination changes that tend to affect pixels within a part uniformly. This makes structural recurrence the basis of the visual summary, addressing a major difficulty in recognizing related content across a long and visually variable record.
neurips-2010-structural-epitome-a-way-to.tldr: A structural epitome summarizes recurring visual structure while accommodating appearance changes such as illumination.

paragraphs: Some datasets are naturally described by a hidden hierarchy, but its branching structure and depth are unknown. This paper proposes a nonparametric prior over such hierarchies. Nested stick-breaking processes allow trees with unbounded width and depth, so the prior does not require a fixed limit on either dimension.

Observations can belong to any node, rather than being restricted to leaves, and the model makes them infinitely exchangeable. The construction can also be viewed as an infinite mixture whose components are related through an evolutionary diffusion down the tree. This gives the hierarchy a role in describing dependencies among mixture components, beyond simply arranging them into groups.

The stick-breaking formulation supports Bayesian inference through Markov chain Monte Carlo methods based on slice sampling. These methods generate samples from the posterior distribution over trees. The authors apply the approach to hierarchical clustering of images and topic modeling of text. The contribution combines a flexible space of possible hierarchies with a sampling procedure for learning about those hierarchies from data.
neurips-2010-tree-structured-stick-break.tldr: Nested stick breaking defines a Bayesian prior over unbounded trees with observations at any node and enables posterior inference.

paragraphs: Kernel dimension reduction was originally developed for supervised problems, where a compact input representation should preserve information useful for predicting responses. This paper adapts that framework to unsupervised learning. The challenge is to formulate an analogous information-preservation objective when there is no separate response variable.

The authors extend kernel-based measures of independence to the setting where the covariates and responses are the same data. These measures guide the construction of a low-dimensional representation. The approach thus carries the motivation of supervised dimension reduction into an unsupervised formulation, using the observed data themselves on both sides of the relationship.

Empirical studies find that the compact representations support meaningful visualizations and clustering. When the representations are subsequently used with supervised classifiers, the methods also produce lower classification errors than the compared state-of-the-art approaches, especially in very low-dimensional embeddings. These results suggest that the learned compression preserves useful structure for both exploratory analysis and later classification in the evaluated settings, even though the representation-learning formulation is unsupervised.
neurips-2010-unsupervised-kernel-dimensi.tldr: An unsupervised extension of kernel dimension reduction produces compact representations useful for visualization, clustering, and evaluated classification tasks.
